analysis.one_liner: Requires standard nutrition labels and truthful health claims on packaged foods.
analysis.headline: The bipartisan Senate bill to put nutrition labels on packaged food cleared its committee in April 1990 but was never brought to a Senate vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have required almost all packaged foods to carry a standard label listing calories, calories from fat, total and saturated fat, cholesterol, sodium, carbohydrates, sugars, protein, and fiber, in serving sizes shoppers actually use. It would have set government definitions for claims like "low fat" and allowed only disease-related health claims backed by scientific consensus, and it would have let states sue to enforce the rules. Its Senate committee approved it, but the bill never reached the Senate floor.
analysis.who_benefits: Shoppers would gain a standardized, comparable nutrition label on nearly every packaged food, letting them see calories, fat, cholesterol, sodium, sugar, and fiber at a glance instead of relying on whatever the manufacturer chose to disclose. Government-defined claim terms would stop marketing language from outrunning what is actually in the box, and state attorneys general could enforce the rules in court. People managing heart disease, high blood pressure, or weight would have the most to gain.

how_it_helps.text: Requires nearly all packaged foods to carry a label stating calories per serving, calories from total and saturated fat, and the amount of total fat, saturated fat, unsaturated fat, cholesterol, sodium, total carbohydrates, complex carbohydrates, sugars, total protein, and dietary fiber.
Standardizes serving sizes to amounts customarily consumed and requires the number of servings per container, so shoppers can compare products on the same basis.

Restricts nutrient-content claims like "low fat" or "reduced sodium" to foods meeting government-defined standards, and allows disease-related health claims only where the Secretary finds scientific consensus, so marketing matches what is actually in the food.
Lets individual states bring court proceedings to enforce the labeling rules, adding enforcers beyond federal agencies.

Sets a firm timetable: a National Academy of Sciences report within six months, proposed regulations three months later, and final regulations six months after that, with the rules taking effect 18 months after enactment.

analysis.who_pays: Packaged food manufacturers would bear the cost of testing products, redesigning labels, and reprinting packaging within 18 months of enactment, and some might reformulate products to keep making claims; part of that cost would likely reach shoppers through prices. Federal and state governments would absorb enforcement costs, and the Secretary of Health and Human Services would carry the burden of the NAS study and rulemaking on a tight schedule.

drawbacks.text: Exempts restaurant food and anything sold for immediate consumption, as well as food prepared in a retail establishment like a deli, so a large share of what people eat would remain unlabeled.
Companies would face label redesign and reprinting costs on an 18-month deadline, which small producers would feel hardest and which could be passed through in prices.
Raw fruits and vegetables would not need on-package labels, only information provided to consumers in a manner the Secretary prescribes, so the produce aisle gets a lighter standard.
Allowing health claims only when the Secretary finds scientific consensus is a high bar that could keep even well-supported claims off labels for years while the regulations catch up.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is one-time compliance costs for food companies against everyday, lasting information for every shopper. The label redesign expense is real but modest against the scale of the packaged food market, and the 18-month phase-in spreads it out. The bill's real design weaknesses are its carve-outs: restaurants, deli counters, and the produce aisle stay outside the mandate, and the scientific-consensus gate on health claims would move slowly. On balance the costs are the ordinary price of a disclosure mandate and the benefits reach every grocery purchase.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate committee approved the bill in April 1990, but nobody ever brought it to the Senate floor for a vote before the Congress ended in January 1991.

narrative.text: Senator Howard Metzenbaum introduced the bill on July 27, 1989, joined by Senator John Chafee, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Labor and Human Resources.
The committee requested comment from the Department of Health and Human Services on September 26, 1989, and held hearings on November 13, 1989.
On April 25, 1990, the committee ordered the bill reported favorably with an amendment in the nature of a substitute.
After the favorable committee order, no further action was taken: the Senate never debated or voted on the bill, and it died when the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Packaged food makers came out ahead: without a Senate vote, they avoided a federal labeling mandate and government-defined claim standards for the rest of this Congress, while shoppers continued to rely on whatever nutrition information manufacturers chose to volunteer.

for.name: Howard Metzenbaum
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and moved it through committee, where it was ordered reported favorably.

for.name: John Chafee
for.what_they_did: Joined Metzenbaum in introducing the bill.

for.name: Senate Committee on Labor and Human Resources
for.what_they_did: Requested executive comment from HHS, held hearings, and ordered the bill reported favorably with an amendment in the nature of a substitute.

against.name: Senate leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a Senate floor vote after the committee approved it in April 1990; no floor action appears in the record before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill itself was bipartisan — introduced by a Democrat and a Republican, cosponsored by 6 Democrats and 1 Republican, and approved by its committee — and no recorded vote ever showed opposition, since the Senate never took one.

industries.note: The bill would force standardized labels on nearly all packaged foods and police nutrient-content and health claims, ending the option to disclose selectively or market with unstandardized language. A mandate's absence means companies keep discretion over what shoppers learn about calories, fat, sodium, and sugar.

Claims like "low fat" or heart-health messages could be made only with government-defined terms and, for disease claims, scientific consensus, sharply limiting marketing latitude. Companies also making compliant claims would be shielded from being regulated as drugs.

Food sold for immediate consumption and food prepared in retail establishments is exempt from the label mandate, and raw produce needs only information provided in a manner the Secretary prescribes. Retailers and restaurants largely escape the compliance burden that packaged food makers would bear.
